items.source: dair-ai Top AI Papers of the Week (November 16 - November 22) - 2026
items.title: Self-Improvement Memory
items.summary: Harness optimization is usually studied with one fixed model and one fixed benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer has to decide which parts of an evolved harness to keep, but the harness code alone does not record why earlier edits were made or how they performed. Researchers from Google Cloud AI, Google DeepMind, and Penn State study this setting, which they call continual recursive self-improvement, and give the harness optimizer its own memory.

items.source: dair-ai Top AI Papers of the Week (November 16 - November 22) - 2026
items.title: AutoRL
items.summary: Reinforcement learning is a central step in improving model capabilities, but automating it is hard because training is unstable and needs constant supervision. Researchers from Meituan and collaborating universities introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system that supervises a live RL run the way an RL researcher would, instead of following a fixed recipe.

items.source: dair-ai Top AI Papers of the Week (November 16 - November 22) - 2026
items.title: Weight-Space Programming
items.summary: Neural networks predict well, but in science the goal is often an explanation, and deep models rarely show which features drive their predictions. Researchers from Microsoft Research and colleagues introduce interpretable weight-space programming (iWSP), where an LLM agent builds models by writing their weights and features directly in code, with no gradient training.

items.source: dair-ai Top AI Papers of the Week (November 16 - November 22) - 2026
items.title: GUARD
items.summary: Agents that edit their own harness without an external grader often get worse over time. Reflection and scalar scores mix up what an edit newly broke with what was never solved, which leads to local regressions, forgotten skills, and bloated memory. Google Cloud researchers propose GUARD, a framework for evolving a harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory around a frozen base model without reference answers.

items.source: dair-ai Top AI Papers of the Week (November 16 - November 22) - 2026
items.title: EfficientSkill
items.summary: Skill optimizers usually add a new rule after every failure. The skill grows, the agent reads more tokens every turn, and long loops start to time out. Researchers from Google and Purdue University introduce EfficientSkill, which learns a skill for accuracy first and then prunes it for length.

items.source: dair-ai Top AI Papers of the Week (November 16 - November 22) - 2026
items.title: Safe Personal RSI
items.summary: A change to a personal assistant's instructions can improve how it handles tasks while also changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports its actions. Researchers from CMU, UC San Diego, UC Berkeley, and other institutions build Safe Personal RSI, an update gate for Kicker, a personal health assistant.

items.source: dair-ai Top AI Papers of the Week (November 16 - November 22) - 2026
items.title: Against All Likelihood
items.summary: This essay from Meta argues that maximum likelihood, the dominant training principle for LLMs, is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth, since unlikely events happen every day and frequently repeated statements can be false. Drawing on philosophers who tie objectivity to invariance, including Nozick, Poincaré, and Cassirer, it proposes judging a statement true when it holds across relevant changes to the environment.
